Rachel's green dress with white cardigan is not what a 1969 Mission Control female support team member wore — they wore conservative knee-length dresses, usually in solid muted colours like navy, grey, or beige, not bright green with a white cardigan. Margaret's purple wool cardigan, cream blouse, brown A-line skirt, tan stockings, and brown lace-up shoes — the shoes are wrong; a 70-year-old woman in 1969 Switzerland would wear low heels or flats, but the more recognizable period piece would be a dress and cardigan set in muted tones, with a hat and gloves for a formal visit. However, "1969 period" for a Swiss grandmother in summer visiting a workplace is a specific recognizable look. The purple cardigan and brown skirt pass, though the shoes being lace-up is odd for a 70-year-old woman — Mary Janes or pumps are more typical. Overall, Lily and Ethan's spacesuits need correction to match the authentic white Apollo suit. James's inflight coverall needs to be white with red trim. Rachel's Mission Control dress should be a more period-appropriate colour and silhouette. Margaret's outfit is borderline but acceptable for a Swiss grandmother in 1969.
2. Drawability — Lily's "white fabric soft cap with a short peak worn clear of the eyes" — "with a short peak" could be drawn as a baseball cap, which is wrong for an Apollo suit. Ethan's "grey fabric soft cap with a short peak" — same issue. Margaret's "brown leather low-heeled lace-up shoes" — low-heeled lace-up shoes are an unusual combination; it could be drawn as an oxford, a brogue, or a boot, creating ambiguity.
3. Colour distinction — Lily's spacesuit is white, Ethan's is silver-grey — these are distinct currently but will both become white when corrected, creating a conflict. James's coverall is light blue (blue), Rachel's dress is green, Margaret's cardigan is purple (purple) and skirt is brown. If Lily and Ethan both wear white suits, their caps, gloves, and boots must provide colour distinction. The mesh of the suit layers or the cap colour can differ.
4. Slot conflicts — None apparent. Lily and Ethan's spacesuits are described as one-piece suits with cap, gloves, and boots — no conflicts. James's coverall with belt and gloves — no conflicts. Rachel's dress, belt, cardigan, pumps, headset — cardigan over dress is an outer layer over top, no conflict. Margaret's cardigan buttoned over blouse, skirt, stockings, shoes — no conflict.
5. Face — Lily's "soft cap with a short peak worn clear of the eyes" — says it is worn clear of the eyes, so no brim shadowing. Ethan's cap similar. No visor or helmet. James's glasses are listed. Rachel's headset is worn over hair, not covering face. No mask or veil. Pass.
6. Completeness — Lily: top and bottom integrated in spacesuit, footwear present. Ethan: same. James: coverall (top and bottom), belt, gloves, boots. Rachel: dress (top and bottom), belt, cardigan, pumps. Margaret: cardigan, blouse, skirt, stockings, shoes. All complete. No tail or nightwear needed.
7. Style world — No world named for style check.
8. Sex — Lily and Ethan both wear the same Apollo spacesuit description. Apollo suits were unisex in shape; the "male and female form" distinction doesn't apply here — the suit is the same garment. No issue. James's coverall is male. Rachel's dress is female. Margaret's outfit is female. All pass.
9. Coverage — No pages put a character in bed or into pyjamas. No transformation (tail, wings, animal form). No missing costume entry. Page 1-3 show Margaret, Ethan, Lily, James in civilian clothes before the launch — but the locked page plan shows them at Mission Control and Kennedy Space Center. The story describes them at Kennedy Space Center for the launch, but the page plan shows Pages 1-2 at Mission Control in Houston, and Page 3 is a wide shot of the Saturn V with no characters. Page 4 is Rachel and Margaret in Mission Control. Pages 5-13 are the costumed children and James in space, with Rachel and Margaret in Mission Control. So the characters are never shown in civilian clothes before the launch in the pages — they go directly from Margaret handing Ethan the paper at Mission Control (Page 1-2, where they are in period dress, not yet costumed) to the space scenes where they are in spacesuits. But the current wardrobe lists them as "costumed" — Lily, Ethan, James in Apollo suits, Rachel and Margaret in Mission Control/period dress. This matches the page plan: Pages 1-2 show them in period clothes (the same clothes they'd wear at Mission Control, since they're at Mission Control). So no missing non-costume category — they are always in their listed outfits on the pages they appear. Wait — Page 1-2: Margaret, Ethan, Lily, James outside Mission Control. They are not in costume yet; they are in the clothes they'd wear as visitors to Mission Control. But the wardrobe only lists "costumed" for Lily, Ethan, James — implying they only wear the spacesuit. If Page 1-2 shows them before the launch, they need a civilian outfit. The story says "Before the launch, Margaret tells Ethan and Lily... she gives Ethan a folded piece of paper." Then "On 16th July 1969, Ethan, Lily, and James launch from Kennedy Space Center." The page plan puts this handoff outside Mission Control in Houston (Page 1-2). So on Pages 1-2, the family is at Mission Control in Houston, not yet launched. They would be wearing 1969 period civilian clothes, not spacesuits. The wardrobe is missing a period outfit for Lily, Ethan, and James. This is a coverage failure.
10. Child coverage — Lily (age 6) and Ethan (age 9) are costumed as Apollo astronauts. Their suits cover the whole body. No swimwear or nightwear. Their costume is a full-body suit. No bare chest, midriff, or one-piece with skirt/tail. Pass for the costume, but they lack civilian clothes for Pages 1-2.
11. Garment variety — If Lily and Ethan both wear identical white Apollo suits with only cap colour differing, that's a recoloured set. They need distinct garment types or silhouette — perhaps one wears the suit with a different configuration (EVA gloves vs. intravehicular gloves, or one with a cooling garment visible). But the Apollo suit is specific; varying it too much breaks recognisability. Distinct cap designs, glove rings, and boots can differentiate them. James's coverall should be distinct from the children's suits.
12. Plot garments — Page 1: Margaret gives Ethan "a folded piece of paper with President Kennedy's 1961 promise written on it." This is a prop (paper), not a garment. Page 11: Ethan holds the open paper. No garment needed. The story says Ethan puts it in his pocket. Ethan's costume has "a chest pocket" — good. Plot garments check passes.
13. Appearance only — No outfits mention page numbers, events, or other characters. All descriptions are garment-focused. Pass.
14. Props — The folded paper is a prop, not a garment. No outfit lists it. Pass.

Summary of faults:
- Check 1: Lily's soft cap with a peak is not Apollo-recognizable. Ethan's suit is the wrong colour (silver-grey instead of white). James's coverall is the wrong colour (should be white, not light blue). Rachel's dress colour may be too bright for 1969 Mission Control; green works but a cardigan worn open over a short-sleeve dress is a specific look — acceptable but the dress silhouette might be improved. Margaret's lace-up shoes are unusual.
- Check 2: Lily and Ethan's caps described as "with a short peak" invite baseball-cap shapes.
- Check 3: When Lily and Ethan both wear white suits, their largest garments share the dominant colour (white). Must differentiate with secondary colours or trim.
- Check 9: Coverage — missing period civilian outfits for Lily, Ethan, and James for Pages 1-2, where they appear at Mission Control before the launch. Rachel and Margaret are already in Mission Control/period outfits, which can serve for Pages 1-2 as well. But Lily, Ethan, and James need 1969 period civilian outfits for those pages.
